```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "100%")
# A number written for the text: plain for moderate sizes, and as
# m x 10^e (HTML) otherwise
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  x <- signif(x, digits)
  if (!is.finite(x)) return(as.character(x))
  if (abs(x) < 1e-300) return("0")
  e <- floor(log10(abs(x)))
  if (e >= -3 && e <= 4) return(format(x, digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
  sprintf("%s &times; 10<sup>%d</sup>", format(x / 10^e, digits = digits),
          as.integer(e))
}
```

```{r setup}
library(onestepcox)
```

## The estimator

`onestepcox` provides closed-form estimators of the hazard ratio of a
two-group comparison of survival data that approximate the Cox partial
likelihood estimator. The main estimator of the package, called MH-Halley,
starts from the Mantel-Haenszel estimate of the log hazard ratio and takes
one Halley step on the Cox score equation. With `eta0` the Mantel-Haenszel
estimate and `U`, `I`, `J`, and `L` the score and its negative first,
second, and third derivatives at `eta0`, the estimate and its standard error
are

```
d    = 2 U I / (2 I^2 + U J)
eta1 = eta0 + d
se   = (I + J d + L d^2 / 2)^(-1/2)
```

The anchor is in closed form and the step is taken once, so no iteration is
needed, and `U`, `I`, `J`, and `L` are computed in the same pass over the
risk sets. Under proportional hazards, the Mantel-Haenszel and Cox estimators
are both root-n consistent for the log hazard ratio, so they differ by a term
of order `n^(-1/2)` in probability. The error of a Halley step is of the third
order in the error of its starting value, so the MH-Halley estimate differs
from the Cox estimate by a term of order `n^(-3/2)` in probability.

## Estimating the hazard ratio

`EstHR()` takes a formula and a data frame, as `survival::coxph()` does, or
vectors of times, event indicators, and group labels. The argument `method`
selects one or more estimators. The example below uses the German Breast
Cancer Study Group data in the `survival` package and compares hormonal
therapy with no hormonal therapy (variable `hormon`).

```{r estimate}
est <- EstHR(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon, data = survival::gbsg,
             method = c("MH_Halley", "MH", "Pike", "Peto", "Cox", "Cox_NR"))
est
```

The treatment group has `hormon` equal to
`r attr(est, "groups")[["treatment"]]` (hormonal therapy), and the control
group has `hormon` equal to `r attr(est, "groups")[["control"]]`: without
the argument `control`, the control group is the smallest value of the group
variable, or the first level of a factor.

`"Cox"` is the estimate of `survival::coxph()` with a tight convergence
tolerance, and `"Cox_NR"` is the Cox estimate computed by Newton-Raphson
iteration on the same risk-set summaries as the closed-form estimators,
until the Newton step is negligible. The MH-Halley estimate of the hazard
ratio is `r sprintf("%.4f", est["MH_Halley", "exp(coef)"])`, and the Cox
estimate (`"Cox_NR"`) is `r sprintf("%.4f", est["Cox_NR", "exp(coef)"])`.
Their log hazard ratios differ by
`r fmt_num(abs(est["MH_Halley", "coef"] - est["Cox_NR", "coef"]))`, and the
Mantel-Haenszel estimate, from which the step starts, differs from the Cox
estimate by `r fmt_num(abs(est["MH", "coef"] - est["Cox_NR", "coef"]))`.

`plot()` draws the estimates and their confidence intervals as a forest
plot. It returns a `ggplot` object, which can be changed further with
`ggplot2`.

```{r forest, fig.alt = "Forest plot of the hazard ratios and their confidence intervals by method for the gbsg data."}
plot(est)
```

## Tied event times and strata

Tied event times are handled by the Efron method by default, as in
`survival::coxph()`, or by the Breslow method with `ties = "breslow"`.
Strata are given with `strata()` in the formula.

```{r strata}
EstHR(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon + strata(grade), data = survival::gbsg,
      method = c("MH_Halley", "Cox_NR"), ties = "breslow")
```

## Vectors instead of a formula

The same estimates can be computed from vectors. The control group is then
given by `control`, and the event indicator is coded 1 (event) and 0
(censored), or TRUE and FALSE.

```{r vectors}
d <- survival::gbsg
EstHR(d$rfstime, d$status, d$hormon, control = 0, method = "MH_Halley")
```

## Risk-set summaries

All methods except `"Cox"` use the same risk-set summaries, which
`RiskTable()` returns: for each distinct event time (within strata), the
numbers at risk in the treatment and control groups (`n_T`, `n_C`), the
number of events in the treatment group (`O_T`), and the total number of
events (`O`).

```{r risktable}
head(RiskTable(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon, data = survival::gbsg))
```

## Further articles

- [Agreement with the survival package](validation.html) compares the
  estimates with `survival::coxph()` and `survival::survdiff()` on data sets
  of the `survival` package and shows how fast the difference from the Cox
  estimate shrinks as the sample size grows.
- [Operating characteristics in simulations](simulation.html) uses
  `GenSimData()` and `CompareOC()` to compare the estimators in simulated
  trials.
- [Large-sample limits and the choice of anchor](limits.html) uses
  `LimitHR()` to show why the step starts from the Mantel-Haenszel estimate
  rather than the Pike estimate.
